title: Timeouts, retries, backoff and jitter
seriesDescription: Language-independent interview topics (concepts, SQL, design, AI engineering): no Java and no Python code or library names.
description: Timeouts on every external call, deadline budgets, retry rules, exponential backoff with jitter, retry amplification, retry budgets and idempotency keys.
source: AWS Architecture Blog (Exponential Backoff and Jitter); Google SRE Book (Handling Overload, Addressing Cascading Failures); Stripe API docs (idempotent requests); nginx proxy module documentation

questions.prompt: Match each HTTP client timeout with the phase it limits.

right.text: Establishing the TCP (and TLS) connection to the server
Waiting for the next chunk of response data
Waiting to acquire a connection from the client pool
Resolving the DNS cache entry TTL

questions.explanation: A slow trickle of bytes can reset a read timeout again and again, so an overall deadline is still needed on top of the per-phase timeouts.

questions.prompt: Write the nginx directives that make a reverse proxy wait at most 2 seconds to connect to the upstream and at most 5 seconds between reads of its response.
questions.explanation: nginx defaults are 60 seconds for both, far too long for an interactive path. proxy_read_timeout limits the gap between two reads, not the whole response, so pair it with an application-level deadline.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: In a call chain A -> B -> C, the timeout for the call from B to C should be shorter than the time A is still willing to wait for B.
questions.reason: Otherwise A gives up while B and C keep working on a result nobody will read, wasting capacity.

whys.a: Correct: If B waits longer than A does, B and C burn capacity on abandoned work.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Propagate a deadline (gRPC deadlines, an X-Request-Deadline header) and subtract elapsed time at each hop.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A client that times out waiting for a payment response cannot tell whether the server processed the payment.
questions.reason: A timeout means the server rolled back everything it did for the request.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Correct: A is true because the response may be lost after the work. R is false: a client timeout says nothing about server-side state.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: This is why mutating calls need idempotency keys: the client can retry safely or query the outcome.

questions.prompt: Write a curl command that POSTs the JSON body {"amount":100} to https://api.example.com/payments with a Content-Type header and an Idempotency-Key header whose value is 7f3a-91.
questions.explanation: The server stores the key with the first response and replays that response for retries with the same key. Generate the key once per logical operation on the client, not once per attempt. Other quoting styles are equally valid.

questions.prompt: A call has a 2 second timeout, 3 attempts in total (1 original + 2 retries), and waits 1 s then 2 s between attempts. If every attempt times out, how many seconds pass before the caller gets the final error?
questions.explanation: 2 (attempt 1) + 1 (wait) + 2 (attempt 2) + 2 (wait) + 2 (attempt 3) = 9 seconds. Always compute the worst case and compare it with the caller's own timeout.

questions.prompt: Exponential backoff uses delay = base x 2^(n-1) for the n-th retry, with base 100 ms and no cap. What is the delay in milliseconds before the 5th retry?
questions.explanation: 100 x 2^4 = 1,600 ms. Delays run 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600. Real systems add a cap and jitter.

questions.prompt: Three services are chained: gateway -> orders -> inventory. Each layer makes up to 3 attempts per call (1 original + 2 retries) when the layer below fails. If inventory always fails, how many calls does inventory receive for one gateway request?
questions.explanation: 3 x 3 x 3 = 27. This multiplication is why retries should happen at one layer only or be limited by a retry budget.

questions.prompt: A client enforces a retry budget of 10 percent of its request volume. In one window it sends 1,000 first attempts and the dependency fails every one of them. At most how many retries may it send in that window?
questions.explanation: 10 percent of 1,000 is 100 retries. Without a budget, 3 attempts per request would triple the load (3,000 calls) on an already failing dependency; the budget caps amplification at 1.1x.

questions.prompt: Full-jitter backoff sleeps a random time between 0 and min(cap, base x 2^attempt), with attempt numbered from 0. With base = 100 ms and cap = 10,000 ms, what is the upper bound of the sleep, in milliseconds, for attempt 7?
questions.explanation: 100 x 2^7 = 12,800 ms, which exceeds the cap, so the bound is 10,000 ms. Past the crossover the bound stays flat, which prevents unbounded waits.

questions.prompt: Thousands of clients lost the same dependency at the same moment. Which retry delay strategy best avoids synchronised retry waves?

options.text: Exponential backoff with full jitter: sleep a random value from 0 up to the capped delay.
options.why: Correct: randomness spreads the clients across the whole interval.

options.text: A fixed delay of one second for every client, so all clients retry at exactly the same instants.
options.why: Identical delays keep the clients synchronised.

options.text: Exponential backoff with no randomness, so every client still doubles its wait in lockstep with the others.
options.why: Clients that failed together still retry together, only less often.

options.text: Retrying immediately in a tight loop until the dependency answers, with no pause between attempts at all.
options.why: A tight loop maximises load on a dependency that is already struggling.

questions.explanation: The AWS Architecture Blog compared full, equal and decorrelated jitter; full jitter does the least total work. Add a retry budget on top.

questions.prompt: Which are sound retry rules for outbound calls? Select all that apply.

options.text: Retry only transient failures such as timeouts, connection resets, 503 and 429 (honour Retry-After).
options.why: Correct: these may succeed on a later attempt.

options.text: Retry non-idempotent POSTs only when an idempotency key is sent.
options.why: Correct: the key makes a repeated request safe.

options.text: Cap total retries with a budget, for example at most about 10 percent of requests.
options.why: Correct: a budget bounds the extra load retries can add.
Client errors do not fix themselves; the same request fails again.

options.text: Retry at every layer of the call chain for maximum safety.
options.why: Layers multiply attempts (3 x 3 x 3) and amplify an outage.

questions.explanation: Retry at one layer (usually the outermost that has context), keep operations idempotent, and combine retries with a circuit breaker.

questions.text: Retries should use {1} backoff with {2} so clients do not retry in lockstep, and a retry {3} should cap the extra load that retries can add.
questions.explanation: Backoff spaces retries, jitter desynchronises clients, budget bounds amplification.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Exponential backoff alone prevents a thundering herd of synchronised retries.
questions.reason: Jitter randomises delays so that clients which failed together no longer retry at identical moments.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Correct: A is false: without randomness the clients still retry together, only at growing intervals. R is true.

questions.explanation: Plain backoff only makes the waves less frequent, not less synchronised.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Retrying at every layer of a microservice chain multiplies the load on the lowest dependency.
questions.reason: Exponential backoff means that the delays double on each retry.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Correct: Both are true, but doubling delays is not why load multiplies; nested attempts are.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Nested attempts multiply (3 x 3 x 3), delays add up. Both matter, for different reasons.

questions.prompt: True or false: an HTTP 400 Bad Request response is a good candidate for retry with exponential backoff.

options.why: A malformed request stays malformed on every attempt.
Correct: 400 signals a caller error that retrying cannot fix.

questions.explanation: 408 and 429 are the usual 4xx exceptions. Classify errors into retryable and non-retryable before wiring a retry policy.

questions.prompt: True or false: when a 429 response carries a Retry-After header, a well-behaved client waits at least that long (plus jitter) before retrying.

options.why: Correct: the server is telling the client when capacity is expected to return.
Ignoring the header and retrying on your own schedule adds load while the server is shedding.

questions.explanation: Retry-After may be a number of seconds or an HTTP date. It overrides the client own backoff when it is longer.
